artifacts.summary: Decides to remove all four sapience MCP write-tool grants (shape i), identifies the exact edits needed to settings-fragment.json, core/mcp-server-ownership.md's carve-out worked example, sapience-write-path.md's Accepted Residual section, plus three additional in-scope sapience-domain files (review-gate-boundary.md, EXTENSION.md, README.md) that also state the stale 11-tool/4-write-tool fact, and flags the pre-existing merge-additivity limitation that leaves this repo's own settings.local.json unchanged by a source-only edit.

memory_candidates.content: When narrowing or closing a permission-grant residual recorded by a rule's own 'Accepted Residual' section, check the full edit surface before concluding only the two files the task description names are enough: grep the extension's whole source tree (every file inside the task's own edit surface) for the same fact the residual states, not just the one worked example named as THE coupling. In this case the dispatch named settings-fragment.json + core/mcp-server-ownership.md's worked example explicitly, but 3 more files inside the same extension's source tree (review-gate-boundary.md, EXTENSION.md, README.md) independently restated the same now-stale tool-count fact and would have gone stale too.

An MCP server's settings-fragment.json permissions.allow entry can be well-formed JSON but match no real tool (e.g. mcp__sapience__sapience, which matches no tool in a 12-tool live surface) -- distinct from the documented 'bare mcp__{server} grants nothing' footgun. This kind of entry is inert cruft that silently survives review because it looks like a normal grant line; worth a dedicated drift-detection check (diff the server's live tool list against the fragment's enumeration) as a future, separately-scoped task.
